channel.title: Raskell - democratisation
channel.description: Notes on agent platforms, platform automation, edge infrastructure, and applied security. Building automation-first platforms that survive production reality.

item.title: A capability, democratised
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Making software used to be reserved for people with a particular privilege: the money to pay a team, or the team itself, or the years it takes to learn to program well enough to build something real. The power I wrote about is that privilege, democratised. Anyone with an idea, a subscription, and the patience to describe what they want can now have it built, and the ones who learn to describe well get a great deal.

Democratised capabilities have a history, and the history has a shape. Nobody who built the printing press or the web could say what people would do with them, and what people did was not on anyone’s plan. It emerged, from millions of small decisions, and it was better for almost everyone, collectively and in the end, even where it was hard for the people in the middle of it. I expect the same of this, with the same caveat; the move to the city is the comparison I keep returning to. And I expect the window in which it is an advantage rather than a baseline to be short, for the reason in the window before the utility.

item.title: Citizen entrepreneurs
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
A friend of mine, an enterprise architect at a large Swiss energy group, answers the tumult in between with the observation that the same tools that threaten jobs make citizen entrepreneurs possible. An ordinary person can use AI to identify a business opportunity, use AI to build the business, and use AI to operate it. The barrier was never only money; it was the ten different competences a business needs on day one, and those are now available by the hour. He took his own idea seriously enough to build a business idea factory, a system that generates and evaluates opportunities. About a week before we talked, someone else announced a project with the same shape on Hacker News, which he took as confirmation rather than competition.

I find it the most hopeful reading of the window, and the one with the most work in it. It assumes the capability really is democratised, which I believe, and it assumes people will take it up, which is the part the window is for.

item.title: Ideas stop waiting
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I have been shipping more this year than in any year before, and the honest explanation is that nothing changed in me. What changed is that the ideas I had carried in the back of my head for years, project ideas, research questions, things I had never properly put into words, now have a way out. Kishi is one: three game engines and a training loop, which would have been a winter of evenings, done in a month beside a day job. The handbook is another.

I am not faster at the things I already did. A whole category of things has moved from some day to this weekend, and the limiting factor is now how clearly I can say what I want. It feels like a once-in-a-lifetime window, and I think it is one, for a reason I set out in the window before the utility. There is a word for what the window gives a person, and I have come round to it: power, in the good sense.

item.title: Power, in the good sense
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The word I have settled on for the feeling in ideas stop waiting is power. Not in the sense the word usually carries, power over someone, but in the plain sense: being capable of doing something, having possibilities, having a moat of your own. Through the AI services anyone can subscribe to, we became powerful.

It is an uncomfortable choice of word at first, and the longer I sit with it the more I like it. We have trained ourselves to hear power only as hierarchy, and to look for a victim in every arrangement that has some. This is a kind of power nobody took from anyone. It was not redistributed; it was created, and handed out to whoever cared to learn it. Capability is power, and it is a relief to say so without apology. What makes it more than a personal feeling is that the capability is democratised, which is where the interesting consequences start.

item.title: The window before the utility
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I argued in The Economics of Inference that tokens are a metered utility, priced per unit like water or electricity, and that pricing and provision will converge on the utility model. The consequence follows: AI capability will be commoditised. It will become normal, boring, and available to everyone on the same terms, and once it is, having it is no advantage at all, any more than having electricity is.

That is the end state. We are not there. The models, the tools and the prices are still moving every quarter, and in a moving market the advantage goes to the people who adopt early and learn to use the thing well, which is work. This is why the feeling in ideas stop waiting is a window and not a new normal: nobody in 2036 will write a note about feeling empowered by their electricity supply. The window is open now, it is once in a lifetime in the literal sense, and what one does with it is the question. One answer is in citizen entrepreneurs.
